name: Northwest Face

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on Cascade River Road ~21.7 mi from Marblemount; NW Forest Pass to park, self-issue wilderness permit required.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 in Marblemount, take the Cascade River Road (FS Road 15) east about 22 miles. Pavement ends near mile 10; the gravel beyond is potholed and gets narrow and steep near the end. The Boston Basin trailhead is a small pullout at about 3,200 ft, just before the Cascade Pass road-end lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and camping in Boston Basin requires a park backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin High Camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on flats below the Boston/Forbidden glaciers; head northwest across glaciated terrain toward the face.
waypoints.directions: From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into Boston Basin to the high camps near 6,400 ft.

waypoints.name: Boston/Forbidden glacier basin
waypoints.note: Rope up and cross the glacier basin toward the northwest aspect of the peak, weaving around moats and crevasses.

waypoints.name: Moat/bergschrund at face base
waypoints.note: Cross the moat/bergschrund at the base of the northwest face, stepping from ice onto rock; often the technical crux of the approach in late season.

waypoints.name: Northwest Face ice band
waypoints.note: ~900 ft of 30-45 degree snow and ice in two sections split by a narrow rock band; front-pointing likely by mid-summer.

waypoints.name: Knife-edge / North Ridge crest
waypoints.note: Steep, somewhat loose 4th-to-low-5th climbing leads to a knife-edge crossed at 5.6 (crux 5.8) where the route joins the upper North Ridge.

waypoints.name: Forbidden Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; descend the West Ridge couloir into Boston Basin.

descent_text: Do not reverse the Northwest Face; descend by the standard West Ridge. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the notch between Forbidden and Torment. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This means NW Face parties do not re-cross the Boston or Forbidden Glaciers or re-climb Sharkfin Col on the way down.

approach_variants.name: All the way round to the Forbidden Glacier's north arm
approach_variants.notes: This is the hardest-to-reach established line on the peak and most parties treat it as three days. The recorded approach goes the long way round: from the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft, often pushing on to a bench near 7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe to the notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse that heavily crevassed glacier, and continue around to the north arm of the Forbidden Glacier on the mountain's other side. Other parties reach the same basin without the Boston Glacier at all — by dropping west off the North Ridge line, by rappelling from the West Ridge notch over crevasses and moats, or over Torment Col. All of them end in the same place. From the north arm, about 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice leads to the base of the rock.
approach_variants.season: Mid summer, for the best balance of firm ice and dry rock
hazards: Two crevassed glaciers before any climbing, with a large crevasse that opens around 7,600 ft in many seasons and can cost real time
A committing rappel off Sharkfin Col — retreat means re-climbing to the col
A moat or bergschrund where the snow pulls back from the foot of the rib
A shaded, cold aspect that holds hard ice late, and a face that tops out at a cornice near 8,375 ft
A descent on a completely different side of the mountain, by the West Ridge couloir
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The deciding fact is which glacier you are standing on, and it settles this route against both its neighbours in one look. This route starts from the Forbidden Glacier's north arm, on the mountain's west side. The North Ridge and the Northeast Face both start from the Boston Glacier, on the east. If your approach ended on the Boston Glacier and you started climbing there, you are on one of those two, not this.

The positive landmark is the rib. From the north arm an obvious rock rib runs roughly 1,800 ft up the face, with ice on both sides of it — the face is two ice sections split by a narrow rock band. You should be able to see a continuous rib rising from where you stand. If what is above you is a broad, undifferentiated snow and ice slope with no rib in it, you are not under this route.

The first-move test is snow, not rock. Above the moat comes roughly 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice before any technical rock. If you stepped off the glacier straight onto rock, you are on the Northeast Face — which begins with 300 ft of rock and only then reaches its ice.

Count the ground above the ice: about 500 ft of somewhat loose 4th to low-5th, soloed or simul-climbed, leads to a knife-edge ridge crossed at 5.6, and the 5.8 crux follows immediately after it. A knife edge is the confirmation that you are on the rib and not on ground beside it.

And the large crevasse at about 7,600 ft is a position marker as well as a hazard — it opens on the approach in most seasons and is the thing most likely to make you detour; note where you crossed it, because you are not reversing this way.
